title: Emotions Station
strapline: A calm corner with mirrors, puppets and faces — somewhere to find out what a feeling is called.
intent: Children learn that feelings have names, and that naming one is the first step to managing it.
Children begin to understand that other people feel differently from them — the root of empathy.
Children build a small set of strategies for expressing big feelings safely rather than physically.
Puppets let a child talk about a feeling at one remove, which is often the only way in.
A predictable calm space gives children somewhere to go before a feeling overwhelms them.
implementation: Set up a genuinely calm area — low light, soft floor, away from the busiest provision.
Provide unbreakable mirrors at child height so children can watch their own face make a feeling.
Stock it with puppets, picture cards of emotions (happy, sad, angry, excited, worried) and sensory toys.
Model using it yourself: name your own feeling out loud in front of the children.
Never send a child there as a punishment — it is a resource, not a naughty step.
Use the cards in the moment when a real feeling happens, not only at group time.
Talk about what helps: a cuddle, a drink, some space, a squeeze of the sensory toy.
key_questions: What does your face look like when you feel like that?
Can you find the card that matches how you are feeling?
What do you think the puppet is feeling, and why?
What helps you when you feel cross or worried?
How do you think your friend felt when that happened?

impact.text: Children name basic feelings in themselves and in pictures and stories.
Children talk about what caused a feeling and what helps them feel better.
Children notice and comfort a friend who is sad or hurt without being asked.
Children reach for strategies that work for them when feelings get big.
Children use words first to sort out a squabble, most of the time.
Children use talk to explain their thinking and resolve disagreements.

enhancements: A photo set of the children's own faces making each feeling, used as the cards.
A feelings check-in at registration where each child moves their name to a face.
A story basket of picture books about big feelings kept permanently in the space.
A "calm-down kit" the children design themselves — what would help you?
A breathing prompt on the wall — smell the flower, blow out the candle.
A worry post-box for children who would rather draw a feeling than say it.

playing_exploring: Children explore feelings safely through puppets and mirrors rather than head-on.
The space is open access, so using it is always the child's own choice.
active_learning: Children return to strategies that worked and use them again unprompted.
Regulating a big feeling takes real persistence, and they build it here.
creating_thinking: Children link cause and feeling — this happened, so I felt that.
They reason about what another person might be feeling and why.
